title: UFOs & Nuclear Surveillance / Biblical Archaeology
excerpt: Author Larry Hancock argued that decades of UFO reports suggest organized alien surveillance of nuclear weapons facilities. Followed by author Dinesh D'Souza, who contended that archaeology increasingly supports Biblical narratives.
content:
About the show

In the first half, guest host Richard Syrett spoke with author Larry Hancock, who argued that decades of UFO reports suggest organized alien surveillance of nuclear weapons facilities. Drawing on 1,200 cases spanning 30 years, Hancock explained that his team applied military "indications analysis" to identify patterns across locations, time periods, and types of encounters rather than treating sightings as isolated incidents. The research, he noted, found a progression from radioactive-materials facilities at Hanford and Oak Ridge, to bomb assembly and storage sites, and later to deployed nuclear weapons and missile installations. "There's no doubt that they had a military interest and they had a focus on the atomic weapons," he remarked.

He contended that early Air Force and CIA officials regarded the UFOs as a potential national-security threat, particularly amid fears of Soviet espionage. The military initially considered whether the objects could be advanced Soviet aircraft built with German technology, but Hancock maintained that explanation did not withstand investigation. He also described reports of green fireballs over New Mexico and Texas near sensitive atomic sites. According to Hancock, institutional resistance grew once some analysts considered extraterrestrial origins. He recalled an Air Force technical group that raised the possibility faced a severe backlash: "They were all removed from their positions," he said. "It was clear early on that nobody really wanted to hear that."

Hancock argued that UFO encounters with military aircraft indicated deliberate signaling rather than direct aggression. In one reported interception, he recounted that an object matched a fighter's speed, followed it after it turned back for fuel, and then left without attacking. "There's some messaging going on here," he observed. "It has the capability to engage our aircraft, but it doesn't."

------------------

In the second half, author Dinesh D'Souza contended that archaeology increasingly supports Biblical narratives. He cited the discovery of King David's palace by archaeologist Eilat Mazar as a prime example of the Bible guiding excavation. D'Souza noted that Mazar used biblical texts referencing Phoenician craftsmen to locate the site before digging began. "She's operating kind of with the Bible in one hand and her spade or trowel in the other... and then she's letting the stones do the talking," he remarked. Discussing the destruction of Sodom and Gomorrah, D'Souza described findings by archaeologist Steven Collins at a northern Dead Sea site. Pottery initially mistaken for Islamic glazing was sent to a lab and identified as "trinitite," a material created by extreme heat similar to atomic blasts. "What may have happened is an explosion from a meteor or an asteroid," he explained, linking it to the biblical description of "fire and brimstone."

On the topic of Noah's Ark, D'Souza acknowledged that the boat-shaped Durupınar formation in eastern Turkey warranted further investigation and was not definitive proof. He emphasized its reported 515-foot length, which he said aligned with the Ark's dimensions using the Egyptian royal cubit. He also presented indirect evidence for the Exodus, including Egyptian art depicting Semitic laborers and the detailed Egyptian cultural knowledge found in the biblical text. D'Souza argued that the writer of Exodus showed "an uncanny, detailed knowledge of the texture of Egyptian life."

Turning to the New Testament, he highlighted a first-century ossuary bearing the name of Caiaphas, the high priest associated with Jesus's trial, and the 1961 Pilate Stone, which identified Pontius Pilate as "Prefect of Judea." D'Souza insisted the Caiaphas discovery was especially personal, claiming that archaeologists were "looking at the actual bones of the guy who put Jesus up on the cross." Regarding the Church of the Holy Sepulchre as the site of Jesus's crucifixion and burial, D'Souza pointed out that initial objections regarding its location inside Jerusalem's walls were resolved as archaeologists realized the ancient city was smaller than previously believed.
